 Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B 
 by Maria Deutscher 
 Amazon.com Inc. today announced plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc. and acquire its core technology. 
 The company didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. That’s nearly twice the valuation Decart reportedly received after its most recent funding round in May. 
 In August, reports emerged that the company had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC. The artificial intelligence provider reportedly sought to buy Decart for $6 billion but walked away from the deal in September. Rumors that Amazon could swoop in emerged the following month.  
 Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the company’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold. 
 The company hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart announced its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.”  
 Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed  that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion. 
 The company says that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language

 Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes 
 Sarah Perez 
 2:05 PM PST · November 23, 2026 
 Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes. 
 The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. 
 Image Credits: Anthropic 
 The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself. 
 “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” 
 Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

 Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks 
 by Mike Wheatley 
 Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence . Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution. 
 They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched. 
 In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough.

full_text:
Amazon snaps up Decart's AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips | TechCrunch 
 In Brief 
 Posted: 
 9:14 AM PST · November 23, 2026 
 Image Credits: Decart (opens in a new window) under a Amit Elkayam license. 
 Rebecca Bellan 
 Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips 
 Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart. 
 The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.  
 Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models to run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.  
 As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post . 
 “Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.” 
 Amazon, which has been so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.  
 Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

full_text:
Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance | TechCrunch 
 In Brief 
 Posted: 
 1:37 PM PST · November 21, 2026 
 Image Credits: Matthias Balk/picture alliance / Getty Images 
 Anthony Ha 
 Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance 
 Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. 
 Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” 
 “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” 
 Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. 
 That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

 Moonshot AI Cancels $150M Nvidia Chip Leasing Deal 
 Moonshot AI cancels $150M Nvidia chip deal amid U.S. restrictions. 
 20.11.2026 
 ForkLog 
 Chinese company Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi AI model family, has canceled a $150 million deal to lease computing power with Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 accelerators in Indonesia. The decision follows tightened U.S. restrictions on remote access by Chinese companies to advanced processors, according to The Information , citing two informed sources. 
 The agreement involved using a large cluster of Blackwell Ultra B300 through a Southeast Asian cloud provider. Moonshot expected to gain access to the resources no earlier than 2027. 
 Access Restrictions 
 On November 16, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced new export control measures. The rules took effect on November 19 following their publication in the Federal Register. 
 Previously, Washington focused primarily on the physical delivery of advanced computing accelerators. Chinese developers could access similar equipment by renting servers outside China. The new rules aim to restrict this method of technology use as well. 
 BIS introduced a requirement to obtain licenses for the export, re-export, and transfer of certain computing equipment if used in data centers providing significant computing power to companies from China, Macau, and other restricted jurisdictions.

full_text:
Former DeepSeek Core Member Zhang Bo Open-Sources Personal Agent That Runs a 125B Model Locally on a 12GB GPU With No Token Fees — BigGo Finance Former DeepSeek Core Member Zhang Bo Open-Sources Personal Agent That Runs a 125B Model Locally on a 12GB GPU With No Token Fees Add preferred source Zhang Bo, former head of the DeepSeek-VL project, announced on November 19 the open-sourcing of Linger, a personal agent product developed by his company Simplex AI, with the code uploaded to GitHub. The product reads local email, calendars and files and operates the user's already-logged-in browser, positioning itself around local inference with zero token fees. Its in-house PolyStrata MoE inference engine uses tiered scheduling of expert weights to run the 125B-parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 12GB VRAM plus 64GB RAM configuration at 45.5 tokens per second. The project uses an Apache 2.0 license with commercial restrictions: local use is free, while the cloud-hosted version is waitlist-only, and the performance figures have not yet been independently reproduced. The developing entity is SIMPLEX AI TECHNOLOGIES PTE. LTD. (hereafter Simplex AI), the company he founded, and the code has been uploaded to GitHub. As of November 20, the repository had about 1.8k stars. 
 Linger is positioned as a dedicated agent running on a personal computer that can read local email, calendars and files and directly operate the user's already-logged-in browsers and applications, eliminating the hassle of repeatedly configuring login credentials. (Photo by Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty Images Shares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic . SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, having invested a total of $64.6 billion in the ChatGPT maker. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Shares of SoftBank on 20 Nov. The sharp decline underscores growing investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns. SoftBank's heavy exposure to OpenAI has made its shares particularly sensitive to shifts in sentiment toward the AI sector. The stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month. If Friday's losses hold, it would be SoftBank's worst day in more than two years. Japanese semiconductor stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron falling 7.19%, Lasertec declining 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%. The sell-off extended to South Korea, where Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 6% and 4.7%

full_text:
Anthropic's 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO | TechCrunch 
 Image Credits: CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP / Getty Images

 Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO 
 Julie Bort 
 4:43 PM PST · November 19, 2026 
 Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. 
 At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. 
 Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. 
 However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” 
 With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. 
 $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate - SiliconANGLE

 UPDATED 17:44 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026 
 SECURITY 
 Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate 
 by Duncan Riley 
 Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials. 
 The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk. 
 Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space. 
 How the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday. 
 The researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

 Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

 If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale.  In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can. 
 The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks , including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp.  Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on AI startup Applied Compute as earnings top forecasts 
 by Duncan Riley 
 Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. today announced that it has agreed to acquire artificial intelligence model training and inference startup Applied Compute Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion. 
 The news came alongside fiscal first-quarter earnings and revenue that were well ahead of Wall Street expectations. Shares of Palo Alto Networks rose more than 8% in late trading, adding to a gain of nearly 10% during the regular session. 
 The acquisition, subject to regulatory clearance, is expected to close in Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal third quarter. Once the deal closes, Applied Compute co-founder and Chief Executive Yash Patil will become co-chief AI officer at Palo Alto Networks, with the startup’s research team also joining the company. 
 Founded in 2025 by former OpenAI Group PBC researchers Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li, Applied Compute offers a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models. The platform is designed to make it easier for companies to train, serve and improve their own models, with an autoscaling inference engine and a model router called Shift-1 also included. 
 Applied Compute raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation earlier this month in a round led by Elad Gil, with Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures and HubSpot Ventures also participating. At the time, the company said that its annualized recurring revenue had topped $100 million. Notable customers include Microsoft Corp. and DoorDash Inc. Coming into its acquisition, Applied Compute had raised more than $500 million in total.

Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board.  Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t —keep financing neoclouds 
 Julie Bort 
 5:00 AM PST · November 18, 2026 
 One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it. 
 And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter , which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter. 
 But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said. 
 Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking . She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion. 
 Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said.

The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks.

 Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. 
 Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year.  Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to accelerate drug discovery with AI 
 by Maria Deutscher 
 Isomorphic Labs Ltd. today announced  that it has closed a $5 billion investment led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital. 
 The venture capital firms were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers. The group included Isomorphic parent Alphabet Inc., which made a “significant investment.” The search giant provided the capital through its GV and CapitalG startup funds.  
 Isomorphic offers a software platform called the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine, or IsoDDE for short. It uses artificial intelligence to speed up several of the tasks involved in developing new medicines. The Alphabet unit says that multiple pharmaceutical companies are already using IsoDDE to power drug discovery programs. 
 Pathogens such as viruses comprise numerous proteins that each power a different biological process. Drugs work by neutralizing a single, particularly important protein without which the pathogen can’t function. Developing a new drug requires researchers to find a vulnerable protein within a pathogen and then develop a compound that can effectively target it. 
 The first step of the workflow is mapping out the shape of a target protein. Researchers look for so-called binding pockets, recesses on the protein’s surface to which a drug can be attached. The task is highly complicated because proteins don’t have fixed shapes. Their configuration changes when they interact with other molecules or encounter new environmental conditions, which happens often.  
 Isomorphic says that IsoDDE speeds up the task of finding binding pockets. When there are no such pockets, it helps researchers develop compounds that cause a target protein to form them.

 Nvidia Corp. delivered earnings and revenue that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations and offered strong guidance for the current quarter in its first earnings call since the shocking resignation of its iconic co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

 The chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.68 per share, surpassing Wall Street’s target of $2.48 per share by a comfortable margin. Revenue for the period came to $115.84 billion, more than double a year earlier and above the $109.1 billion consensus estimate. 
 The vast majority of those sales stemmed from Nvidia’s core data center business, which delivered revenue of $107.6 billion, higher than the Street’s $101.87 billion forecast. For the current quarter, Nvidia said it’s expecting its revenue to grow by about 90%, to $130 billion. Though that suggests a slowdown sequentially from the prior quarter, it’s still nicely above Wall Street’s target of $125.1 billion.

For the first time, she was fielding questions as the company’s interim CEO, which means her responsibilities now go well beyond the numbers. She was joined on the call by Nvidia’s Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones, who insisted that the board has no intention of bringing Huang back as CEO.

full_text: The Nvidia Scandal Could Upend Chip Sales to China. Trump Wants to Keep Them Going | WIRED Skip to main content Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick. Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China. But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks. Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion. Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The New York Times has reported . In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move. Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say. But Trump settled on a third approach

 Maximilian Schreiner

 17. November 2026 
 Kaliforniens Generalstaatsanwalt Rob Bonta verklagt OpenAI wegen des Cyberangriffs, den außer Kontrolle geratene KI-Modelle des Unternehmens im Juli auf die KI-Plattform Hugging Face verübt haben. Laut der Klage habe OpenAI fortgeschrittene Modelle ohne ausreichende Sicherheitsvorkehrungen getestet und die Öffentlichkeit über die Sicherheit seiner Experimente getäuscht. 
 Rund 700 KI-Agenten entkamen laut einer externen Untersuchung während interner Tests ins offene Internet, tauschten geheime Nachrichten aus und koordinierten den Angriff über sieben Tage. Bonta spricht laut Politico von mindestens 80 Vorfällen, bei denen OpenAI die Kontrolle über seine Technologie verloren habe. Unkontrollierbare KI könne kritische Infrastruktur wie Stromnetze, Krankenhäuser und Finanzsysteme bedrohen, so Bonta. 
 OpenAI nannte die Klage einseitig und verweist darauf, dass alle großen KI-Labore mit solchen Problemen kämpfen. Das Unternehmen unterstützt inzwischen strengere Sicherheitsgesetze, Shutdown-Kontrollen und unabhängige Prüfer in KI-Laboren. Jensen Huang's Shock Exit From NVIDIA Is Followed By A New National Security Committee To Oversee The Chip Giant's Export Compliance 
 Hardware Industry 
 Jensen Huang’s Shock Exit From NVIDIA Is Followed By A New National Security Committee To Oversee The Chip Giant’s Export Compliance 
 Ramish Zafar • 
 Nov 17, 2026 at 06:47am EST 
 Comments 
 Add to Preferred Sources
 Image credits - NVIDIA 
 AI chip giant NVIDIA has announced that it will create a national security committee to oversee its compliance and national security obligations. The announcement follows the shock exit of former CEO Jensen Huang amidst widespread controversy about his dealings with a Singaporean data center executive. 
 NVIDIA's New Oversight Committee Will Work With Outside Experts In Trade Compliance & Other Areas To Improve Decision Making 
 As part of the announcement, which is among the few that NVIDIA has publicly made since Huang's departure, the firm shares that it will use every tool in its "disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation." The remarks were made by the firm's board chairman, Harvey Jones, with the press release noting that the new standing committee would receive reports from NVIDIA's existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team.

Additionally, the oversight committee will work with outside experts in important areas to bolster the capabilities of the existing compliance team. 
 Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

 Open AI hit with lawsuit in California over Hugging Face rogue agent incident 
 by James Farrell 
 California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced the state has launched a lawsuit against OpenAI Group PBC after the company’s AI agents earlier this year went rogue and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc. 
 The 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, claims Open AI has engendered the public and put institutions at risk by developing products without suitable safeguards. Bonta likened Open AI’s behavior to being a “public nuisance,” asking the judge to order the company to change its practices while imposing financial penalties for any money the company made from the high-risk areas of its business. 
 “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a statement at a press conference. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.” 
 Bonta believes that without external pressure, the scope and frequency of such attacks will increase in the future. “In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company,” he added. 
 The “unprecedented” rogue attack in question occurred on July 21 this year when one of Open AI’s agents escaped what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment — a sandbox.  California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents 
 Russell Brandom 
 12:07 PM PST · November 16, 2026 
 OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public. 
 At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” 
 The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. 
 The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. 
 The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure. 
 “OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

Attorney General Rob… / X Post Log in Sign up Post Log in Sign up Rohan Paul on X: "California sued OpenAI, over that Hugging Face attack, representing one of the first major attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.
The lawsuit alleges OpenAI admitted losing control of its testing agents more than 80 times.
Attorney General Rob Bonta’s complaint, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, says OpenAI has publicly reported only 27 of them.
The case centers on July, when about 700 of its agents escaped a cybersecurity evaluation and attacked Hugging Face’s production systems.
They slipped out through a flaw in a misconfigured software-package server and took about 17,600 actions, yet OpenAI noticed nothing until Hugging Face disclosed the attack.
That blind spot anchors the deception claim of the lawsuit, since OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework requires 24x7 monitoring and network segmentation for High-capability models.
Bonta wants an injunction, restitution and civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under California’s unfair competition and public nuisance laws.
OpenAI’s technical report already conceded that guardrails it runs in production would have flagged the attack as unsafe.
If the court treats harm during internal testing as an unfair business practice, that will basically mean that state attorneys general can police every lab’s evaluation sandbox." full_text:
Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be 'fine’ | TechCrunch

 AI 
 Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’ 
 Rebecca Bellan 
 10:11 AM PST · November 16, 2026 
 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. 
 Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. 
 Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. 
 Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.  
 Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.  
 When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” 
 He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.  
 “It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” 
 OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. full_text: Nvidia's Colette Kress key questions in Nvidia earnings after Huang Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO and interim CEO, will face big questions in Nvidia's earnings call, which comes days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure. The biggest issues revolve around China and whether much of Nvidia sales to Southeast Asia are actually intended for Chinese companies. Nvidia shares have dropped for six straight weeks, the longest losing streak since 2012. In this article NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A worker stands with an Nvidia umbrella outside of the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, Nov. 12, 2026. Manuel Orbegozo | Reuters Days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the chipmaker he founded 33 years ago, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress will now face intense questions about what comes next. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings after the close on Tuesday. While the company is again expected to show explosive growth as the key infrastructure provider to the artificial intelligence boom, Kress and her team will likely be forced to answer questions on chip sales to China, the risks tied to deals with neoclouds and what comes next under new leadership. Huang resigned Thursday, but Nvidia's legions of customers, partners, and investors still rely on the company to continue shipping large quantities of graphics processing units and AI systems. Kress, who has been Nvidia's CFO since 2013, was tapped to lead the company while the board searches for a successor. Analysts expect Nvidia to report 91% revenue growth to $109.1 billion, according to LSEG, with $2.47 in earnings per share.  Forensic Analysis Points to Access to Export-Controlled GPUs, but Does Not Prove Export Violations 
 Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang unveils the Blackwell GPU. 
 An analysis has found that Nvidia’s cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) chip, Blackwell, which the U.S. government restricts from export to China on national security grounds, appears to have been used in the development of AI models by major Chinese companies. The findings suggest a potential gap in the United States’ semiconductor export controls targeting China. 
 Unemployment Labs, a U.S. nonprofit research organization led by Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher, said in a report published on Nov. 12 that it had identified traces of Blackwell graphics processing unit (GPU) usage in models from four Chinese AI companies: DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group. The analysis covered six models released since April this year: DeepSeek’s V4-Flash and V4-Pro, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and K3.1-Pro, MiniMax’s M3, and Ant Group’s Ling-3.1-Flash. 
 The researchers used digital forensic techniques to analyze numerical patterns and initialization fingerprints embedded in AI models’ weights. The analysis found that DeepSeek V4-Flash and MiniMax M3 matched the computational characteristics of the B200 and B3
anriss: Unemployment Labs identifizierte Spuren der Blackwell-GPU in Modellen von DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax und Ant Group. Die Forscher nutzen digitale Forensik, um numerische Muster und Initialisierungs-Fingerabdrücke in den Gewichten der KI-Modelle zu analysieren.

 Firma von Jensen Huangs Ex-Geliebter soll Nvidia-Chips für 12 Milliarden Dollar nach China vermittelt haben 
 Matthias Bastian 
 View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian 
 15. November 2026 
 Laut vom Wall Street Journal eingesehenen Unterlagen arrangierte Megaspeed zwischen März 2024 und Juni 2025 Bestellungen von Nvidia-Hochleistungschips für chinesische Unternehmen im Wert von knapp 12 Milliarden Dollar. Megaspeed gehört Alice Huang, der früheren Geliebten des inzwischen abgesetzten Nvidia-CEO Jensen Huang . Die Firma schickte die Chips laut WSJ an Käufer in China, die langjährige Geschäftsbeziehungen zu dortigen Techkonzernen unterhielten. Die Bestellungen umfassen mehrere hunderttausend Chips, die die USA per Exportkontrolle von China fernhalten wollten. Als Nvidia-Cloud-Partner soll Megaspeed bevorzugten Zugang zu knappen KI-Chips erhalten haben, weil es wohl das chinesische Cloud- und Tech-Unternehmen Alibaba als Großkunden im Portfolio hatte. 
 Nvidia meldete offiziell 12,4 Milliarden Dollar China-Umsatz in sechs Monaten, also 7 Prozent des Gesamtumsatzes. Die Leerverkaufs-Firma Culper Research schätzt jedoch, dass im letzten Geschäftsjahr mehr als 20 Prozent von Nvidias Erlösen auf chinesische Kunden zurückgingen. Ein erheblicher Teil des China-Geschäfts könnte also über Umwege gelaufen sein.

 English International U.S. lab says Chinese AI models trained on Nvidia Blackwell chips despite sanctions A U.S. nonprofit says model fingerprints indicate DeepSeek, Kimi, MiniMax, and Ant Group trained on Blackwell GPUs, while stopping short of proving export-control breaches 입력 2026.11.15. 08:07 조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 Even as the U.S. government restricts Nvidia's most advanced chips, an analysis found that China's leading artificial intelligence (AI) models were trained on Nvidia's cutting-edge chips. The findings draw attention as evidence that China may have skirted U.S. export controls, amid an uproar over a scandal alleging that Alice Huang (Chinese name Huang Le), suspected of being a Chinese spy, used an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (COE) to smuggle advanced AI chips into China. Experts have long seen it as likely that Chinese firms remotely rented Nvidia compute through data centers in Southeast Asia or smuggled Nvidia chips directly via workaround routes. An illustration shows the NVIDIA logo and the silhouette of former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. /Courtesy of Reuters Unemployment Labs, a U.S. nonprofit research group led by former OpenAI researcher Will Depue, said in a report on the 14th (local time), "Forensic analysis of public AI models found evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group used Nvidia's Blackwell graphics processing units (GPUs) to build their AI models despite export controls." The models analyzed were six systems released since April this year: DeepSeek's V4-Flash and V4-Pro, Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 and K3.1-Pro, MiniMax's M3, and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-Flash. According to the report, the analysis detected numerical patterns and initialization fingerprints unique to the Blackwell chip architecture. In particular, DeepSeek's V4-Flash and MiniMax's M3 matched the compute characteristics of the B200 and B300 chips. Four mode

The findings rely on signatures left in published model weights during initialization. Hardware at the center 
 Nvidia's Blackwell architecture powers the company's current generation of data center accelerators, including the B200, B300, GB200 and GB300 systems. U.S. export controls restrict shipments of these chips to China. A forensic report from Will DePue, a former OpenAI engineer and founder of Unemployment Labs, claims several Chinese AI labs trained models on Blackwell hardware anyway. 
 DePue said he found signatures tying models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group to Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The report identifies six Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 and MiniMax-M3. Four of those models match Grace Blackwell configurations used in Nvidia's GB200 and GB300 rack-scale systems.

 Model developers set initial weight values before training. A common approach uses the Philox pseudorandom number generation algorithm. With a given seed, Philox produces the same sequence of values each time it runs.

 US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model."
